title: Biggest US Law Firms Explore Selling Stakes to Private Equity
pub: Financial Times, 6 August 2026 — captured from the Australian Financial Review syndication of the FT report
author: Stephen Foley · Kaye Wiggins · Suzi Ring

dom.t: Outside capital: Permission does not create investable firms

st.t: Outside capital: Permission does not create investable firms
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by distinguishing broad interest from active or completed investment and by arguing that firms should accept outside capital only when they can identify a credible use and concrete long-term benefits. It provides evidence of exploratory market activity, not proof of investability or improved outcomes.
qs: Holland & Knight attorney Trisha Rich, whose practice helps structure MSO deals to comply with ethics rules, said they had talked to half of the largest firms in American Lawyer’s Am Law 100 ranking, but a much smaller group was actively exploring the possibility of taking outside capital.
“Every firm needs to be able to answer the question, what are you going to do with the money?” she said.

kp.k: Major US firms explore outside capital without committing
kp.d: The 6 August 2026 report, citing people with knowledge of the matter, identifies Paul Weiss, Quinn Emanuel and Proskauer as exploring private investment through conversations with investors or bankers. White & Case has senior lawyers examining the structure. These are exploratory activities rather than announced transactions: sources describe Quinn Emanuel's discussions with Guggenheim Securities as research, while Paul Weiss explicitly says it is not currently pursuing the proposal.
qs: Paul Weiss, Quinn Emanuel and Proskauer are among firms to have had conversations with private equity groups or bankers to consider taking outside capital, according to people with knowledge of the matter.
Several of the people cautioned that no decision had been taken and the firm had not committed to a sale process, but was simply carrying out research.
“There have been no follow-up meetings and this is not something we are currently pursuing.”
White & Case has a group of senior lawyers examining the structure.

kp.k: MSOs separate legal work from administration to enable investment
kp.d: The report describes management services organisations as a proposed route around US professional restrictions on nonlawyer ownership by separating legal work from administrative functions. It cites medicine and accounting as precedents for the structure, while reporting that its application to law remains untested and could encounter regulatory problems; the article does not establish regulatory acceptance.
qs: But some investors are stepping up their attempts to break into the legal industry using a structure known as a “management services organisation”, which separates a firm’s legal work from its administrative functions to get around the rules.
Buyout groups have already used the MSO model to circumvent similar professional ethics rules on outside ownership of medical practices and accountancy firms.

Some private equity groups are also wary of law firm investments, partly fearing that AI could harm business models and because the MSO structure is untested in the legal profession and could hit regulatory problems.

kp.k: AI investment plans coexist with investor disruption fears
kp.d: The report places law firms' interest in outside capital in the context of substantial spending on talent and planned AI investment. Conversely, some private equity groups reportedly fear AI could damage law-firm business models. These are reported plans and concerns, not measured AI effects or demonstrated investment outcomes.
qs: Law firm leaders are increasingly keen to understand the model and how it could reshape their industry when many are spending large sums on top talent and planning to invest in AI.

Some private equity groups are also wary of law firm investments, partly fearing that AI could harm business models and because the MSO structure is untested in the legal profession and could hit regulatory problems.

kp.k: Vesting equity could retain and recruit rainmaker partners
kp.d: Discussions at US-based firms reportedly consider using an MSO structure to retain high-revenue partners through equity vesting over time or attract competitors' stars. The report also records sceptics' contrary expectation that private equity backing could repel powerful partners and cause departures. Neither outcome is presented as established.
qs: Discussions at US-based firms have focused on whether the MSO structure could help in the war for talent, either to lock in rainmaker partners with equity that vests over time or lure other firms’ stars.
Sceptics say powerful partners might be turned off by the prospect of working for a private equity-backed firm, risking an exodus.

kp.k: Outside ownership raises intergenerational and governance concerns
kp.d: Some law-firm leaders reportedly worry that a transaction would be perceived as older partners cashing out at younger generations' expense. Others fear lawyers would lose control over resource-allocation decisions. The report presents these as concerns about prospective deals, not documented consequences.
qs: Some law firm leaders are also concerned the move could be seen as older partners cashing out at the expense of younger generations, while others fear lawyers losing control of decision-making about how the firm should allocate resources.

kp.k: Broad interest exceeds active pursuit of outside capital
kp.d: An unnamed MSO adviser characterises firms as interested but reluctant to move first. Holland & Knight attorney Trisha Rich, whose practice structures MSO deals for ethics compliance, reports conversations with half of the firms in the Am Law 100, but says a much smaller group is actively exploring outside capital. This is a practitioner's account of discussions, not a reported survey or count of completed investments.
qs: “Everyone is interested, but everyone wants to go second,” said one adviser specialising in MSO structures.

Holland & Knight attorney Trisha Rich, whose practice helps structure MSO deals to comply with ethics rules, said they had talked to half of the largest firms in American Lawyer’s Am Law 100 ranking, but a much smaller group was actively exploring the possibility of taking outside capital.

kp.k: Accounting acquisitions motivate New Mountain's legal-market exploration
kp.d: The report identifies New Mountain Capital, with $US60 billion ($85.1 billion) in assets under management, as having met Paul Weiss at the investor's request. Its law-firm MSO exploration followed acquisitions of two major accounting firms using a similar structure. People familiar with its thinking say it has not committed to a legal-sector deal.
qs: Executives at Paul Weiss met New Mountain Capital, a private equity group with $US60 billion ($85.1 billion) in assets under management, at the investor’s request in New York recently, people familiar with the matter said.
New Mountain began exploring law firm MSOs after acquiring two major accounting firms using a similar structure, though people familiar with its thinking say it has not committed to doing a deal.

kp.k: Capital raising should demonstrate long-term firm benefits
kp.d: Rich recommends that firms identify how they would use outside capital and articulate its long-term benefits before proceeding. Her advice makes a clear strategic use for the money a condition for pursuing an MSO transaction, rather than endorsing investment for its own sake.
qs: “Every firm needs to be able to answer the question, what are you going to do with the money?” she said.
“If you do not have an answer that crystallises the long-term benefits to the firm, then you probably should not be doing this.”

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Planned AI investment forms part of the context for major US law firms' interest in outside capital, while possible AI disruption makes some private equity investors wary of investing.
pts.d: The FT reporters describe law firm leaders' growing interest in management services organisation (MSO) structures against a backdrop of substantial talent spending and planned AI investment. This is a contextual association, not a demonstrated claim that AI is causing firms to sell stakes. Separately, they report some unnamed private equity groups' concern that AI could harm law firms' business models. The article does not specify the mechanism of that potential harm or predict particular changes to staffing, billing, productivity or legal service quality.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is qualitative reporting about investment discussions and concerns, rather than measured AI effects.
pts.d: The reporters document exploratory outside-capital discussions involving Paul Weiss, Quinn Emanuel and Proskauer, citing people with knowledge of the matter. These discussions support the broader account of interest in private investment, but do not establish AI's causal role. The AI investment plans and investor fears are reported without named speakers, spending figures, benchmarks or concrete examples of AI-induced business-model damage. Paul Weiss's quoted response qualifies the broader investment story by saying it is not currently pursuing the structure.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: AI spending is prospective as of the report's 6 August 2026 publication; possible business-model harm has no specified horizon.
pts.d: The source describes firms as planning AI investment and investors as fearing potential harm, not reporting realised AI disruption. Outside-capital interest remains exploratory and qualified by widespread hesitation. Investor wariness is only partly attributed to AI; uncertainty about MSO structures and regulatory problems is an additional stated reason. No timetable is given for AI investment, any resulting market changes or completed US law firm transactions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The AI-related claims concern large US law firms and prospective private equity investors.
pts.d: For large law firms and their leaders, planned AI investment is part of the strategic context in which outside capital is being considered. For some private equity groups, the possibility that AI could undermine law firm business models contributes to investment caution. The source does not identify which named firms' discussions were specifically motivated by AI, or which named investors expressed the AI concern. It offers no direct AI-impact claim about clients, the public, access to justice or particular lawyer roles.
